text: Denner was so exact that he painted the almost invisible fuzz of hair on smooth skin. He came from Altona, the only son among eight children of a Mennonite minister and dyer, and an accident at eight left him with a limp. Slow recovery bored him, so he began to draw and to copy Berchem and Bloemaert. When he showed his portrait of an old woman to Adriaen van der Werff, Van der Werff could only compare it with the Mona Lisa. The painting went to Charles VI, the Holy Roman Emperor, and Denner received 5875 guilders for it.

Born in Springfield, Ohio, Boggs settled in Montmartre in Paris. He studied at the École des Beaux-Arts and was a pupil of Jean-Léon Gérôme. In 1923 he became a naturalised French citizen. Among his paintings are The Windmill of the Galette and a view of Notre-Dame from the Pont au Double. His work is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Van Gogh Museum and the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University.

Jansson was known as the blue painter, because of his night-time views of Stockholm in shades of blue. His father was a postal messenger and a skilled amateur flautist. Scarlet fever at fourteen left him with bad eyesight and hearing and chronic kidney problems. He couldn't afford Paris, so he stayed in Stockholm, which gave him most of his motifs, and his first trip outside the Nordic countries came only in 1900. A committed socialist, he helped found the Artists' Union in 1886. From about 1904 he mostly painted male nudes.

Born in a log cabin on his father's farm in Ohio, Whittredge came from a family that had earlier lived in New England, where his father was a sea captain. He became a landscape painter of the Hudson River School and was friends with Albert Bierstadt and Sanford Robinson Gifford. He travelled widely. For a year he was president of the National Academy of Design. He also sat on the selection committees for the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition and the Paris Exposition of 1878.

Conder's father wanted him to become a civil engineer, against the boy's artistic inclinations. As a child he spent several years in India, until his mother died in Bombay when he was four. At 16 he was sent to Sydney to work for his uncle, a land surveyor. He later became a key figure in the Heidelberg School, which is arguably the beginning of a distinctively Australian tradition in Western art. He worked as a painter, lithographer and designer.

Turchi went by the nickname L'Orbetto. He trained in Verona with Felice Riccio, called Brusasorci, and when Riccio died he and fellow painter Pasquale Ottino completed a series of the master's unfinished canvases. He painted the organ shutters for the Accademia Filarmonica of Verona. Later he went to Venice to work for a while under Carlo Cagliari. His style has been called soft and Caravaggesque at once, and late in life he moved to Rome.

Mignon began his training in his native Frankfurt, where his family, originally from Hainaut, owned a shop. When the family moved to Wetzlar, he was placed in the care of Jacob Marrel, a flower painter. He later moved to the Dutch Republic and worked in Utrecht during the last part of his short life. He painted flowers, fruit, game, fish and garlands, and the influence of Jan Davidsz. de Heem shows in them. Collectors of the highest rank across Europe sought his work.

Albert Zimmermann came from Zittau and had three brothers who were also painters, Max, Richard and Robert. He was Max's teacher. He was mostly self-taught, though he did study at the academies in Dresden and Munich. Lake Constance and the Swabian Alb are among the subjects of his landscape paintings. He died in Munich in 1888, at the age of eighty.

Schinkel was six when his father died in the great fire of Neuruppin. Later he studied in Berlin with Friedrich Gilly, who became a close friend, and with Gilly's father, David. He became the architect who shaped Berlin, with buildings like the Altes Museum, a model for national art museums elsewhere. His Bauakademie is considered a forerunner of modern architecture. He also painted. He designed furniture and stage sets too.

Russell is known as the cowboy artist, and he made more than 2,000 paintings of cowboys, Native Americans and landscapes in the western United States and Alberta. He also made bronze sculptures. He was a storyteller and author too. He backed the landless Chippewa in their bid to get a reservation in Montana, and in 1916 Congress passed legislation creating the Rocky Boy Reservation. The Russell museum in Great Falls, Montana, holds over 2,000 of his works and personal objects.

Calvert made small wood engravings in the late 1820s, and no one outside his circle of friends saw them until his son published them in 1893, in an edition of 350. He was born in Appledore in Devon, spent a spell in the Navy, then studied art at Plymouth and the Royal Academy Schools. William Blake inspired his early visionary work. He belonged to The Ancients, the Blake-influenced group that met at Samuel Palmer's house in Shoreham. He also made etchings, and he visited Greece in 1844.

Verster came from an artistic family: his father administered the National Museum of Natural History in Leiden and painted birds. He studied at the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague, alongside Breitner, Isaac Israëls and Willem de Zwart. For ten years he shared a studio in Leiden with a still-life painter who later became his brother-in-law. Until about 1885 he painted in the Hague School style. Then he met Jan Toorop and other artists of Les Vingt in Brussels and began working with rough brushstrokes and intense colour. He had success with large floral still lifes and landscapes.

Hanneman spent sixteen years in England, where Anthony van Dyck influenced him and Constantijn Huygens introduced him at court. Back in The Hague he married Maria van Ravesteyn, the daughter of his old drawing teacher. In 1656 he was one of the dissenters who split off to form the Confrerie Pictura, and he headed it at first. He is best known for his portraits of the exiled British royal court. Like many Catholic painters, he fell on hard times and sold possessions again and again in 1670. His entire estate brought only 1,000 guilders.

A vicar's son from Korpilahti, Cawén grew up with parents who loved music and art. He studied in Helsinki, then in Paris. In 1912 he went back to Paris and travelled on to Brittany and Spain. Late in 1916 he became a founder member of the November Group, a Finnish group of expressionists and cubists. He painted altarpieces for churches in Mänttä, Kuusankoski, Lapinlahti and Simpele. He lived at Ilola near Porvoo, his mother's childhood home.

Buchanan trained as a calico pattern designer in Scotland, with botany as a hobby. He emigrated to Dunedin in 1852 and worked as a survey assistant and gold prospector during the Otago gold rush. Joseph Dalton Hooker suggested him to James Hector, who employed him in 1862 as botanist and draughtsman for the Otago survey. He kept that job at the Colonial Museum in Wellington, now Te Papa, and for twenty years took field trips all over New Zealand. He was a fellow of the Linnean Society.

Brend'amour came from a Huguenot family in Aachen and was the youngest son of a police inspector. He learned wood engraving from 1846 to 1849 as an apprentice to the Cologne engraver Eustach Stephan. He paid for more training at the Cologne art school by copying older woodcuts, such as Holbein's Dance of Death and Dürer's twelve apostles. In 1856 he founded a wood-engraving studio in Düsseldorf. He is regarded as a pioneer of modern woodcut technique.

Moreelse spent most of his life in Utrecht, where he trained with the Delft portraitist Michiel van Mierevelt. A study trip to Italy brought him many portrait commissions. Back home he joined the saddlers' guild, which then included painters, and in 1611 he co-founded the new Guild of St Luke with Abraham Bloemaert and became its first dean. Commissions came from across the Dutch Republic. Besides portraits he painted a few history pictures in the Mannerist style.

Turner and Thomas Girtin were among Malton's pupils. He is called the younger to tell him apart from his father, an architectural draughtsman and writer on geometry. He was with his father when the older man lived in Dublin. Then he spent three years in the London office of the architect James Gandon. In 1782 he won a Royal Academy gold medal for a theatre design. He mostly exhibited views of London streets.

Guérin's Return of Marcus Sextus excited wild enthusiasm at the Salon, partly because viewers saw in it an allusion to the turmoil of the French Revolution. The painting shows a victim of Sulla's proscription coming home to find his wife dead. The president of the institute publicly crowned Guérin on the occasion. He had already won one of three grands prix in 1796, as a pupil of Jean-Baptiste Regnault. Poor health forced him to leave Rome, and he went to Naples, where he painted The Shepherds in the Tomb of Amyntas.

The details of Bout's life are not well established. Most sources say he was baptized in Brussels in 1658, but that was a different Pieter Bout, and he was probably born there in the 1640s. Nobody knows who taught him. He became a master in the Brussels Guild of Saint Luke in 1671. He painted landscapes and city views in a style like Jan Brueghel the Elder's, with a clear, soft palette that looks ahead to the 18th century, and he often worked with other Flemish painters.

Eleanor and Summer are among Benson's best-known paintings, and they show his daughters outdoors at the family's summer home, Wooster Farm, on North Haven island in Maine. He started out painting portraits of distinguished families and murals for the Library of Congress. He studied at the School of the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, and in 1883 he went to Paris to study at the Académie Julian. Wildfowl and landscapes filled his oils, washes, watercolours and etchings. A native of Salem, Massachusetts, he painted as an American Impressionist.

Ramberg's drawings of scenes in the Harz Mountains reached George III, who was also Elector of Hanover. In 1781 Ramberg was introduced to the king and made humorous sketches and caricatures for him. George urged him to go to London and supported him there. He studied with Benjamin West. In 1784 he won a silver medal for life drawing and drew the Academy's exhibition itself.

Lagrenée the elder studied under Carle van Loo and won the Grand Prix de Rome in 1749. In 1755 the Académie royale elected him a member. He showed promise in drawing and painting from an early age. His younger brother Jean-Jacques was a painter too. Among his works are Mary with the Child and the Young John the Baptist, Mars and Venus as an allegory of peace, and The Triumph of Flora.

A carpenter's son from Frankfurt on the Oder, Werner began an apprenticeship as a decorative painter in 1857. He then studied at the Prussian Academy of Arts in Berlin and at the academy in Karlsruhe. He painted the Franco-Prussian War and the unification of Germany in a realist style. All three German emperors, William I, Frederick III and Wilhelm II, favoured him. He joined the Prussian Academy in 1874.

Floris went to Italy and came home to Antwerp in 1545 as a leading painter of the city, then at the height of its prosperity. He belonged to the Romanists, northern painters who studied Michelangelo and Raphael in Italy and absorbed what they saw. History paintings, allegorical scenes and portraits were his main subjects. He also designed tapestries and made prints. Many of his works for churches were destroyed in the Beeldenstorm of 1566.

Zhao Mengfu descended from the Song imperial family, but he lived under the Yuan. He was recommended for an audience with Kublai Khan in 1286, yet he received no important position. Later the Yuan emperor Renzong greatly appreciated his work. He was a calligrapher and scholar as well as a painter, and he belonged to the Academy of Worthies. His wife, Guan Daosheng, painted too.

Carlone preferred painting to sculpting, though his father was a sculptor, and he was placed with Giulio Quaglio. He later studied in Venice and Rome, with Francesco Trevisani, until he was 23. Then he went north and left oil paintings and frescoes in Ludwigsburg, Passau, Linz, Breslau, Prague and Vienna. In Vienna he painted the ceiling images in the Upper Belvedere. He painted ceilings.

For most of her career Gwen John worked in France. In her lifetime her work was overshadowed by that of her brother Augustus and her mentor and lover Auguste Rodin. Her paintings are mainly portraits of anonymous women, in a range of closely related tones. She was born in Haverfordwest, the second of four children of a solicitor with a dour temperament. Her reputation has grown.

Boissonnas ran the family photographic studio in Geneva from 1887 to 1920. His father had founded it and later settled the family in a building on the quai de la Poste. His work is considered crucial for the development of photography in Greece, and it was used to publicise the country's expansionist ambitions early in the twentieth century. He had seven children. His views of Lake Geneva and Mont Blanc are among his early pictures.

Nobody agrees when Griffier was born. Houbraken says 1656, English accounts make him up to ten years older, and in 1700 he was registered in Leiden as 48 years old. He learned landscape painting and engraving from Roelant Roghman in Amsterdam. He was admitted to the London Company of Painter-Stainers in 1677 and worked in England for at least two decades, including for the Dutch painter Jan Looten. Rhineland landscapes and views of the English countryside were his subjects.

Palma Vecchio means Palma the Elder, a name that tells him apart from his great-nephew Palma il Giovane, also a painter. His real name was Jacopo Negretti. He was born near Bergamo, but his recorded career took place in or near Venice. He is first recorded there in 1510, though he had probably been in the city for some time. He was perhaps apprenticed to Andrea Previtali, another Bergamo man, and his earlier works show the influence of Giovanni Bellini.

The Asa Tarbell House in West Groton, Massachusetts, beside the Squannacook River, was Tarbell's birthplace. His father died of typhoid fever contracted while serving in the Civil War. His mother remarried. Tarbell joined the Ten American Painters and was a leading member of the group known as the Boston School. His work is in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, the Metropolitan Museum and the National Gallery of Art.

Poccetti started out decorating facades and ceilings in Florence, and he enrolled in the painters' guild for that work in 1570. People also called him Bernardino delle Grottesche, delle Facciate or delle Muse. He first worked in the shop of Michele Tosini. In the 1580s he took part in decorating the Chiostro Grande of Santa Maria Novella. He painted frescoes for the Palazzo Capponi too. He also made etchings.

Hokushū used five signatures over his career. He signed Shunkō until 1818, when he changed his name to Shunkōsai Hokushū. For a single print in 1811 he signed Shōkōsai and announced a change of name. He studied with Shōkōsai Hambei and may also have studied with Hokusai. He was the most important artist in Osaka in the 1810s and 1820s, and he established the Osaka style of actor prints.

Some sources wrongly call Aertgen van Leyden a brother of Lucas van Leyden. Lucas was the son of a painter, while Aertgen, according to Karel van Mander, was the son of a Leiden fuller. In 1516 he became an apprentice to the Leiden painter Cornelis Engebrechtsz, whose style influenced his early work. He also designed stained glass. His works are in the Rijksmuseum, the Metropolitan Museum and the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza.

Boulanger met Victor Hugo in 1824, the year he was among the finalists for the Prix de Rome, and they stayed friends for life. He painted Hugo's daughter Léopoldine at the age of four. Born in Piedmont, where his father was a lieutenant colonel in Napoleon's army, he joined the École des Beaux-Arts in 1821 and trained under Guillaume Guillon Lethière. There he befriended Achille Devéria. He also worked as a poet and lithographer.

Hohlwein trained and worked as an architect in Munich before he switched to poster design. His high tonal contrasts and interlocking shapes made his work instantly recognisable. His forms were sharply defined and his colours bright, with humor and textured patterns. By 1925 he had already designed 3000 different advertisements, and most of his work was made between 1908 and that year. He was a pioneer of the Sachplakat style.

Pforr died of tuberculosis at 24, before his art was recognised. He got his first training from his father, the painter Johann Georg Pforr, and from his uncle Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Younger. In 1810 he left the academy in Vienna for Rome with other students, among them Johann Friedrich Overbeck. They were looking for lost spirituality in their art, and they lived in an abandoned monastery, Sant'Isidoro. He belonged to the German Nazarene movement.

A flag bearer's son from Gorinchem, Verschuring cared more for art than soldiering, so he was sent to learn drawing at eight. At thirteen he became the pupil of Jan Both and stayed six years. Then he left Utrecht for Rome, drawing every place he stayed, especially new buildings. His work was in demand in Venice, so he stayed in Italy for ten years. His landscapes often show soldiers on horseback.

At eight years old Gérard became Jean-Honoré Fragonard's sister-in-law, and at fourteen she went to live with him. She became his pupil in the mid-1770s, studying painting under him and learning drawing and printmaking too. Together they made nine etchings in 1778. Historians now believe she was the sole artist of five of them. More than 300 genre paintings, 80 portraits and several miniatures have been documented to her. She was also the aunt of the artist Alexandre-Évariste Fragonard.

Italy drew Bryullov early. His father was the academician, woodcarver and engraver Pavel Briullo, of Huguenot descent. Despite twelve years at the Imperial Academy of Arts, Bryullov never fully embraced the classical style his mentors taught. After he finished he left Russia for Rome, where he worked until 1835 as a portraitist and genre painter. At the Academy he had been a promising and imaginative student.

Van Son painted mainly fruit still lifes, but he also did flowers, banquets and vanitas pictures. He is known to have painted fish still lifes representing the Four Elements. With figure painters he collaborated on garland paintings, in which a garland of fruit or flowers frames a devotional image. Nobody knows who taught him. Jan Davidsz de Heem clearly influenced him. He was baptized in Antwerp Cathedral in 1623 and buried in the city in 1667.

Motonobu turned the Kanō school into what it is today, through his political connections, patronage, organization and influence. The school trained a great majority of Japanese painters throughout the Edo period. After he died he was called Kohōgen. The Kanō family are presumed to descend from warriors of the Kanō district, in what is now Shizuoka Prefecture. Its forebear Kanō Kagenobu reportedly painted Mount Fuji for a visit by the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshinori.

Sustris was known in Italy as Alberto de Olanda, Albert of Holland. He came from Amsterdam and reached Venice only after he was over forty. Nobody knows his training. Titian's studio used him to paint landscapes, and he travelled with Titian to Augsburg, where he painted portraits. Back in Venice he fell under the influence of Parmigianino and Andrea Meldolla. His son Friedrich and the painter Girolamo Muziano were his pupils.

Nicknamed De Friesche Adelaar, the Frisian Eagle, De Geest learned painting from his father, a stained glass worker, and later studied with Abraham Bloemaert. From 1614 to 1618 he travelled in France and Italy, and in Rome he joined the Bentvueghels. He married a niece of Saskia van Uylenburgh, Rembrandt's wife. In 1634, just before Rembrandt's own marriage, Rembrandt visited his studio.

Hoorn was where Henstenburgh was born and died. According to Johan van Gool he copied prints so well that his parents let him become a pupil of the painter Johannes Bronckhorst. Bronckhorst also worked as a pastry baker, and Henstenburgh learned that business from him and took it over when Bronckhorst died. Nicolaas Verkolje drew his portrait in the album of Joanna Koerten. He is known for fruit and flower still lifes, with a specialty in insects.

Nicolas Mignard spent most of his active life in Avignon, painting religious and mythological scenes for churches and stately homes, and he ended his career as court painter in Paris. He came from a family of artisans in Troyes. His younger brother Pierre became one of the leading French painters of the 17th century and a rival of Charles Le Brun. Nicolas learned from a local master whose name is unknown. Then he went to Fontainebleau to copy the Mannerist painters.

Cantagallina came from Sansepolcro and is best known for etchings of landscapes and religious subjects, influenced by Paul Bril. On a trip through the Low Countries and France in 1612 and 1613 he made detailed pen and wash drawings of buildings, houses and city views. He filled the foreground with people at work or play. His eye caught courtly celebrations and the peasant world alike. Jacques Callot was reputed to be his pupil.

Wilson began in 1849 as a portrait miniaturist in Aberdeen and switched to portrait photography three years later. He got a contract to photograph the royal family, working for Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. He was born in Alvah, Banffshire. In the 1860s he turned largely to landscape photography. He pioneered techniques for photographing outdoors and for the mass production of prints, and by 1864 he claimed to have sold over half a million copies.

An embroidery maker's son, Picard studied at the École des Beaux-Arts under Jean-Léon Gérôme for two years. Paul Philippoteaux noticed him and picked him as one of five assistants to help paint panoramas for exhibition in the United States. His first individual showing came at the Salon in 1888. Later he worked with Henri Gervex and Alfred Stevens on a triptych. He was of Jewish ancestry.

After his father's death in 1816, Martens decided to become an artist and studied landscape painting under the watercolourist Copley Fielding. His father was an Austrian-born merchant who first came to London as Austrian consul. Two of his brothers, John William and Henry, were artists too. In 1832 Captain Blackwood of HMS Hyacinth asked him to join a three-year cruise to India as topographical artist. Later he worked on HMS Beagle, and in 1835 he arrived in Australia, where he painted until he died.

Born in Warsaw to a mapmaker father of German extraction, Jerichau-Baumann began at nineteen to study at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, then one of the most important art centres in Europe. Her early subjects came from Slovak life. In 1844 she first attracted public attention while exhibiting there. After she moved to Rome she mostly painted local life. She married the sculptor Jens Adolf Jerichau.

Huguet was orphaned in 1419 and moved from Valls to Tarragona to stay with his uncle Pere Huguet, who was also a painter. When they moved to Barcelona he met modern trends. He worked in Zaragoza between 1440 and 1445, and later in Tarragona, where the Flemish style of Luis Dalmau influenced him. He kept painting into his mid-seventies. His Consecration of Saint Augustine is in the Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.

In 1755 Smart came second to Richard Cosway in a Society of Arts drawing competition for boys under fourteen. The same year he started at William Shipley's new drawing school in London, along with Cosway and Richard Crosse. He specialised in portrait miniatures. He became president of the Society of Artists in 1778. He went to India in 1788 and got a number of commissions there.

Hallé won the Prix de Rome in 1736 and studied at the French Academy in Rome under Jean-François de Troy until 1744. He came from a family of artists, and his father was Claude-Guy Hallé. As a history painter he received royal commissions for the Grand Trianon, Choisy and the Petit Trianon. He also worked for the Gobelins and for the King of Poland. Among his Roman subjects are The Death of Seneca and The Justice of Trajan.

Nothing is known about when or where Catena was born. The earliest record of him is an inscription on the back of Giorgione's Laura, which calls him the painter's Cholego. His early style is much closer to Giovanni Bellini than to Giorgione, and Giorgione's influence showed only a few years after Giorgione died in 1510. About a dozen signed paintings by him survive. Only one, the Martyrdom of St Christina in Santa Maria Mater Domini in Venice, can be dated with any certainty, to 1520.

Lumsden made some 350 etchings between 1905 and 1946, and most are held at the Burnaby Art Gallery in British Columbia. He always printed his own plates. He travelled to India several times and is noted for his prints of Benares on the Ganges. He studied under Frank Morley Fletcher at Reading Art School and briefly at the Académie Julian in Paris. In 1908 he took a job at the Edinburgh College of Art.

Monamy specialised in marine art. He was baptised in the church of St Botolph's-without-Aldgate in London, the last of five children. His father came from Guernsey, and his grandfather André had been a committed Parliamentarian and one of Guernsey's governors during the 1650s. His mother, Dorothy Gilbert, was the daughter of a Master of the Worshipful Company of Gunmakers. The family name seems French in origin.

Jorde studied under Gerhard Munthe and Harriet Backer, among others, and he also studied in Paris and Italy. In 1905 he moved to Lillehammer, and in 1912 into a house that Thorvald Erichsen had built, designed by Arnstein Arneberg. He lived there until he died. He did decorative work for the Vingrom Chapel and for Granheim Sanatorium in Follebu. In 1925 he decorated Sjøli Chapel.
